identity.title: History of prior abdominal surgery (adhesion risk)

technique.how: Ask specifically about any previous abdominal or pelvic operation (including laparoscopic, gynecologic, hernia repair and appendicectomy), radiotherapy, and prior episodes of obstruction; inspect for scars, which patients may not mention.
technique.prerequisites: None; corroborate with old records or inspection of the abdomen.

interpretation.positive_finding: Prior laparotomy is the dominant risk factor for adhesive small bowel obstruction; in the OMGE series it was the most efficient historical item (RR 12.1) and is one of the best history predictors in the 2013 meta-analysis.
interpretation.negative_finding: A 'virgin abdomen' makes adhesive SBO much less likely and shifts the differential toward hernia, malignancy, volvulus, Crohn's or gallstone ileus, which more often need operation.
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients forget minor or remote procedures; laparoscopy and pelvic surgery also cause adhesions. The item is a risk factor, not a diagnostic sign, and most patients with scars presenting with pain do not have SBO.
interpretation.changes_what: With distension/vomiting: lowers threshold for CT and NG decompression. No prior surgery with SBO features: expect non-adhesive cause and earlier surgical involvement.

estimates.population: 1,333 patients with acute abdominal pain in the OMGE prospective survey (Finland)
estimates.reference_standard: Final diagnosis by OMGE Research Committee criteria
estimates.quote: The most efficient symptoms in the diagnosis of acute small-bowel obstruction were previous abdominal surgery (relative risk (RR) = 12.1)

sources.citation: Eskelinen M, Ikonen J, Lipponen P. Contributions of history-taking, physical examination, and computer assistance to diagnosis of acute small-bowel obstruction. A prospective study of 1333 patients with acute abdominal pain. Scand J Gastroenterol. 1994;29(8):715-721.
Taylor MR, Lalani N. Adult small bowel obstruction. Acad Emerg Med. 2013;20(6):528-544.

Bohner H, Yang Q, Franke C, Verreet PR, Ohmann C. Simple data from history and physical examination help to exclude bowel obstruction and to avoid radiographic studies in patients with acute abdominal pain. Eur J Surg. 1998;164(10):777-784.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not let a prior-surgery history anchor the diagnosis on adhesions when signs of strangulation, hernia, or malignancy are present; do not dismiss SBO in a patient without prior surgery.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: SBO features with fever, tachycardia, peritonism or lactate rise indicate strangulation: fluids, antibiotics, immediate surgical consultation regardless of adhesion history.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: History item with good reproducibility when asked directly; recall of remote or laparoscopic procedures is incomplete.

extraction_notes: Taylor & Lalani 2013 pooled estimates for prior abdominal surgery (their Table) are behind a paywall and not visible via PubMed/PMC; the abstract confirms previous surgery is among the best history predictors. Bohner 1998 abstract lists previous abdominal surgery among six high-sensitivity variables without numbers. Only visible number is the Eskelinen 1994 relative risk (12.1), entered with sens/spec/LR null. A verifier should replace with the pooled LR+/LR- from Taylor & Lalani.
